nodes.title: Plans Board and Treasurer’s Office
key_items: B. The Office of the State Treasurer
nodes.summary: The Plans Management Board acts as fiduciary and has ultimate oversight of the Plans. Its 11 members include four public members and two state employees appointed by the Governor, plus five ex-officio members: the State Insurance Commissioner, State Treasurer, and Secretaries of Education and Finance, and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget. The Board has standing Audit and Governance and Investment Committees, whose members include Board members and outside subject-matter experts. The Board and each committee meet at least four times annually. The Office of the State Treasurer (OST) is the Board’s administrative arm and coordinates Board and committee meetings. OST’s Contributions and Plan Management division markets and promotes the Plans, oversees vendors, and performs certain Plan operations.

nodes.title: C. Deferred Compensation Program
nodes.summary: The voluntary Deferred Compensation Program provides State employees supplemental retirement security beyond statutory pension and benefits (29 Del. C. § 6051). It includes the IRC § 457(b) Plan, § 403(b) tax-sheltered annuity Plan, and § 401(a) employer Match Plan, administered on one recordkeeping platform; the recordkeeper or affiliates/third parties serve as trustee for 457(b) and Match assets and custodian for 403(b) assets. The 457(b) Plan covers eligible regular full- and part-time State employees, excluding temporary workers and consultants, and receives no State contributions. Employees contribute through salary reduction, subject to federal limits, with age-50 catch-ups and larger pre-retirement special catch-ups; contributions may be pretax or Roth, and eligible plan funds may be rolled over. Distributions follow separation, age 59½, or unforeseeable emergency; most required minimum distributions begin at 72, and loans are prohibited. Investments are limited to insured bank accounts, U.S. government debt, regulated insurance/annuities, registered investment funds, and exchange-traded securities. At year-end 2020, it had about $841 million, 10,048 active contributors, and 16,570 positive-balance accounts. The 403(b) Plan covers most public-school, education-department, Delaware Tech, and Delaware State University employees; the State contributes nothing.

nodes.title: 457(b) Plan Overview
nodes.summary: The State’s supplemental 457(b) Plan is available to eligible regular full- and part-time employees, excluding temporary workers and consultants; the State contributes nothing. Employees contribute through salary reductions, subject to federal limits ($19,500 stated), with age-50 catch-up contributions ($6,500) or, instead, special catch-up contributions during the three years before retirement (up to $39,000). Contributions may be pretax or Roth, and certain eligible-plan distributions may be rolled over. Distributions are allowed after separation from employment, beginning in the calendar year the participant turns 59½, or for an unforeseeable emergency; required minimum distributions generally begin at 72, and loans are prohibited. Investments are limited to federally insured bank savings, U.S. government debt, regulated life insurance or annuity contracts, registered investment funds, and securities traded on specified exchanges. The plan is cited at 29 Del. C. § 6057A. At December 31, 2020, it held about $841 million; 10,048 participants were actively contributing and 16,570 accounts had balances over $0.

nodes.title: 2. The 403(b) Plan
nodes.summary: The 403(b) supplemental retirement plan covers most part- and full-time employees of Delaware public schools, the Department of Education, Delaware Technical Community College, and Delaware State University; the State contributes nothing. Employees contribute through salary reductions, subject to federal limits ($19,500, plus $6,500 catch-up at age 50 or older), and may choose pretax or Roth contributions or roll over eligible retirement-plan distributions. Withdrawals generally require separation from employment, age 59½, or qualifying hardship; required minimum distributions usually begin at 72. Loans ended in 2009, though certain earlier vendor loans were grandfathered. Formerly managed locally with over 100 vendors, the plan adopted a formal document and centralized oversight under the Deferred Compensation Council in 2009, which restricted options to Vendor and 13 legacy vendors. In 2016, the Board selected Vendor as sole recordkeeper for ongoing contributions and transferred some legacy assets. At December 31, 2020, about $195.5 million was on Vendor’s platform and $296.7 million remained in legacy assets, for which the Board has limited obligations. The platform had 5,626 active contributors and 7,002 unique account holders; there were 6,863 legacy accounts.

nodes.title: 3. The Match Plan
nodes.summary: The Match Plan is a §401(a) defined-contribution plan established in 2001 and frozen since mid-2008. State and State-supported-instrumentality employees may participate after enrolling in the 457 Plan and contributing for six months; temporary employees and consultants are excluded. Subject to legislative appropriations, the State contributed $10 per pay period from 2001 to 2008, when contributions were suspended; resumption is uncertain. Distributions are allowed after employment ends or upon retirement at retirement age; required minimum distributions generally begin at 72, and loans are prohibited. At year-end 2020, the plan held $25.6 million for 8,991 participants. Participant contracts issued before January 2009 (“orphan” accounts) are excluded from the 403(b) Plan under federal labor guidance. The voluntary, participant-directed DC Program offers a diversified, three-tier investment architecture. Tier 1’s default target-date funds follow glide paths toward more conservative allocations and are selected by anticipated retirement year. Tier 2 offers active and passive core funds across major asset classes and a vendor fixed account; participants may self-manage or pay for professional management, currently through Morningstar.

nodes.title: Match Plan and Investment Architecture
nodes.summary: The Match Plan is unavailable to temporary employees and consultants. Subject to legislative appropriations, the State contributed per pay period for participants deferring to the 457(b) Plan: $10 from January 2001 to July 2008. Legislation suspended contributions in 2008, and none have resumed; whether or when they will resume is unclear. Distributions are allowed after employment ends or upon retirement at retirement age; required minimum distributions generally begin at 72, and loans are prohibited. At December 31, 2020, the plan held about $25.6 million for 8,991 participants. The DC Program is voluntary and participant-directed, offering a diversified, multi-tiered range of investment options with varied risk/reward characteristics. Tier 1’s default options are target-date retirement funds, which gradually shift toward more conservative allocations as the stated retirement date approaches. Participants choose a fund by selecting the anticipated retirement year that best suits their financial goals.

nodes.title: Tier 2 – Core Options
nodes.summary: Tier 2 offers actively and passively managed core funds across major asset classes and a Vendor fixed account. Participants may select and allocate investments themselves or pay additional fees for professional management, currently by Morningstar. Match Plan contributions are limited to rollovers from another IRS §401(a)-qualified plan. Tier 3 provides a self-directed brokerage window, currently through TD Ameritrade, for participants seeking a broader investment range and able to manage their own portfolios. The 457 and Match Plans allow individual stocks and bonds, ETFs, and mutual funds; the 403(b) Plan allows mutual funds only. Participants may pay annual program-manager and brokerage-firm fees. Attachment 6 provides current investment-lineup details, and the investment architecture and options are periodically reviewed under the Board-approved Investment Policy Statement in Attachment 8.

Cyber Responsibilities, Liability and Insurance
A. Vendor Protection of Customer Data
1. The awarded vendor shall, at a minimum, comply with all Delaware Department of Technology and Information (DTI) security standards identified in this Request for Proposals and any resultant contract(s).
B. Definitions
Data Breach
1. In general the term “data breach” means a compromise of the security, confidentiality, or integrity of, or the loss of, computerized data for the State of Delaware that results in, or there is a reasonable basis to conclude has resulted in :

nodes.title: 1. 1 The unauthorized acquisition of personally identifiable information (PII); or
nodes.summary: A data breach includes unauthorized acquisition of personally identifiable information (PII), or access to PII for an unauthorized purpose or beyond authorization, but excludes investigative, protective, or intelligence activities of U.S. federal, state, or local law enforcement or U.S. intelligence agencies. PII is information that alone or combined identifies or authenticates an individual, including names, contact details, credentials, government and account numbers, biometric, criminal, citizenship, medical, and financial information, usernames, and security answers; it also includes information defined as personal information under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act or applicable Delaware law. Customer Data includes text, sound, software, and image files supplied to the vendor by or for Delaware in connection with the contract. A Security Incident is unauthorized access to Customer Data maintained, stored, or transmitted by Delaware or its representative.

nodes.title: C. Responsibilities of Vendor in the Event of a Data Breach
nodes.summary: Upon confirming a data breach, the vendor must notify Delaware DTI and GSS without unreasonable delay, describing the breach, potentially affected record count, and data involved. If the State or vendor determines a breach occurred, the vendor must promptly take reasonable steps to mitigate harm and implement appropriate corrective actions. DTI has final approval over actions restricting, altering, or severing electronic-data access; emergency actions may be taken immediately but require DTI approval to become final. For every confirmed breached record, regardless of who discovered it and notwithstanding the statutory PII definition, the vendor must notify affected individuals as required by Delaware law, deliver a written report on the breach’s nature, extent, and root cause within two business days of notice, and promptly meet with DTI and GSS about remediation. The vendor bears all investigation, response, and recovery costs, including credit monitoring, mailing, website, and toll-free call-center services.

2. Covered Disclosure
2.1 The disclosure of Customer Data as a result of a successful Security Incident.

nodes.title: E. Cyber Liability Insurance

nodes.title: 6. Confidential Information of the State.
nodes.summary: The section defines Confidential Material broadly, whether marked or not, and limits the Vendor’s use and disclosure to contract performance and authorized, need-to-know employees bound in writing. Copies, electronic storage, retention, and disclosure are restricted; legally compelled disclosure requires prompt notice to OST, reasonable protective efforts, and identification of the State’s interest. Exceptions cover public, lawfully obtained, unrestricted, or independently developed information. The Vendor must safeguard material, promptly report breaches or suspected intrusions, and, within six months after termination, return or permanently destroy it at OST’s option, subject to protected legally required retention and requested certification. The State need not disclose material and may seek injunctive relief. The section also requires correction or re-performance of noncompliant services, pass-through or fulfillment of third-party product rights, and Vendor defense and indemnification for specified claims. Public entities retain their legal rights, defenses, and immunities, including sovereign and qualified immunity.

nodes.title: 6. Confidential Information of the State. (intro)
nodes.summary: Confidential Material includes all agreements, documents, and data containing the State’s confidential information, whether or not marked confidential. The Vendor may use it only to perform its contractual duties and may share it only with employees who need access and have been informed of and acknowledged its strict confidentiality obligations in writing. Copies require OST’s written permission, except reasonable copies needed for performance. The Vendor generally may not store or aggregate the material electronically, but may keep files as permitted while performing its duties and for a reasonable period afterward; it must then return or destroy all copies under the referenced provisions. Disclosure to others requires OST’s prior written consent unless required by law. The Vendor must promptly notify OST in writing of court orders, subpoenas, or discovery requests, object and take reasonable protective measures at OST’s request, and mark any material disclosed under legal compulsion to identify its confidentiality and the State’s interest.

nodes.summary: Confidentiality obligations do not cover information already public or later public without breach, unrestricted information already held or lawfully obtained from other sources, or information independently developed without reliance on confidential material. Vendor must take commercially reasonable measures to safeguard confidentiality and integrity, and immediately notify OST of breaches or suspicious intrusions, identifying compromised information and its amount. Within six months after termination, Vendor must, at OST’s option, return or lawfully destroy all confidential material; electronic deletion must be permanent under NIST-approved methods, and Vendor must provide a destruction certificate if requested. Legally or policy-required retention is permitted, but retained data must remain protected under surviving agreement obligations and be destroyed when retention ends. The State need not disclose requested material and may refuse. The State may seek injunctive relief for noncompliance, in addition to other remedies, because damages may be inadequate. nodes.summary: Vendor is an independent contractor, not an employee, agent, or partner of OST, the Board, or the State, and cannot bind them. Vendor personnel receive no State employee benefits, and Vendor must provide their liability insurance. Section 11 is reserved. Either party may terminate for material default after at least 30 days’ written notice and an opportunity to cure and consult; the State may terminate for convenience on 60 days’ notice. Vendor receives payment for services earned through termination and must cooperate in transition at no State cost. A breach termination found unjustified becomes a convenience termination. Intended-surviving obligations, including indemnity and confidentiality, remain; contractual remedies supplement legal remedies. OST may terminate without liability for improper gratuities and pursue breach remedies. Performance is subject to specific legislative appropriations; absent funding, OST may terminate immediately, and unfunded State obligations end without liability.

nodes.title: 13. Assignment; Subcontracts.
nodes.summary: Vendor may not assign or transfer any interest in the Agreement without OST’s prior written consent; an unauthorized transfer is void. nodes.title: 14. Complete Agreement.

If a term is invalid or unenforceable, it is modified as necessary while preserving the rest of the agreement and the parties’ intent. nodes.title: 15. Miscellaneous Provisions.

No commission-based solicitation is permitted, with breach allowing annulment without liability. The agreement is neutrally construed as jointly drafted. At OST’s option, disputes may first be negotiated in good faith by authorized officials, with negotiation communications generally confidential, privileged, and inadmissible. Unresolved disputes may, at OST’s discretion, go to mediation under State law and venue; proceedings and outcomes are confidential as legally permitted, and parties bear their own costs and split mediator fees. Parties are excused from liability for delays or defective performance caused by unforeseeable events beyond their control, absent negligence or willful misconduct. Vendors liable for a breach bear response and recovery costs, including at least three years of credit monitoring.
